paras: The killing of Primus Johnson was the death of a Black man at Shell Mound, on the Tallahatchie River in Mississippi, in early August 1882, during a white posse's pursuit of a Black man accused of attacking a white planter. A telegraphic report said the posse captured Johnson and a mob shot him dead, while a Mississippi paper said he was killed trying to escape from officers.

According to the telegraphic item, on Tuesday, August 1, two brothers it called 'desperado brothers,' William and Henry Morville, both 'colored,' attacked a planter named Matthew Beck. Beck's son shot and killed Henry. The Brookhaven Ledger gave a different version, in which 'a young white man named Beck' killed a Black man named Morrell who had assaulted him with a hoe.

A posse of white men then pursued William Morville and, by the telegraphic account, was fired on by Morville and his friends. The posse captured Johnson, described only as 'colored,' and 'the mob shot him dead'; no accusation against Johnson himself was stated. The Brookhaven Ledger placed his death on the day after Morrell's and said he was killed 'while trying to escape from officers who had him in custody,' without naming who fired.

The telegraphic report closed by saying that whites were 'expecting an attack from the negroes.' A separate Ledger brief described a 'serious negro riot' near Shell Mound the same week, with three Black people killed and three wounded so far as reported, without naming them. No report of an inquest, arrests or prosecution for Johnson's death appears in the coverage.

The Morning Journal and Courier ran the story on August 3 as one short paragraph among its 'Telegraphic Jottings,' after items on a yellow fever death and baseball scores. In Mississippi, the Brookhaven Ledger carried two short items on August 10, one calling the deaths a 'double killing' and the other blaming the 'riot' on 'two turbulent negroes who had long been a terror to the peaceable citizens of that section.' Both papers took the white side's account as given, and only the out-of-state item used the word 'mob.'

The accounts differ on how Johnson died: the telegraphic item says a mob shot him after his capture by the posse, while the Ledger says officers held him and he was killed trying to escape. They also differ on the first killing, naming the dead man Henry Morville or Morrell and the target of his alleged assault as the planter or his son. The Ledger's account is later and more local, but it cites no witness or official finding for the escape.

reader.title: Killing of Primus Johnson
bases: The only telegraphic account says a white posse captured Johnson and 'the mob shot him dead' (A9); a later Mississippi brief instead says he was killed trying to escape officers (A12).

A9 reports a captured Black man shot dead by a mob that had formed as a posse after an alleged attack on a white planter, which meets the standard definition; A12 recasts the death as a killing during an escape from officers, so legality is contested (A9, A12).

Two independent reports agree that a Black man named Johnson was killed on the Tallahatchie after the killing of a Black man by a young Beck, but one says a mob shot him after capture (A9) and the other that he was killed escaping officers (A12).
